title: The Wall and the Cartoon: from the Painter's House at Dusseldorf to an Apocalypse Without a Building
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Dusseldorf, birth in the painter's house
stops.date_confidence: contested year. German Wikipedia gives the precise day-date 23 September 1783; the English Wikipedia infobox and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica both give 1784. The earlier and more precise date is carried, the conflict is not resolved here.
stops.campa: Peter Cornelius is born at Dusseldorf into a house that belongs to the trade. His father, Johann Christian Alois Cornelius, paints and serves the electoral gallery as its inspector; his mother is Anna Helena Corsten. The boy grows up inside the institution rather than beside it, among pictures hung for the instruction of other men's sons. The year itself is contested: the German encyclopedia says 1783 and names the day, the English sources answer 1784, and no document reachable here settles which the family wrote down.
suggested_refs: Baptismal registers of Dusseldorf parishes for 1783 and 1784, which would settle the disputed year

stops.name: Dusseldorf, the academy in his father's shadow
stops.date_confidence: traditional. de.wikipedia has him training at the Dusseldorf academy from boyhood; no source consulted gives a matriculation date, so the year is a placeholder inside his adolescence. Coordinate corrected to Eiskellerstrasse 1, approximately 51.2288/6.7716; the pool's 51.2251/6.7768 lies some 500 m southeast.
stops.campa: He is set to drawing before he is set to anything else, and enters the Dusseldorf academy among the men his father works beside. The instruction is the late eighteenth century's: the cast, the correct contour, the antique taken at second hand and finished smooth. He learns it thoroughly, and he will spend the rest of his life arguing against the taste that produced it. The building the academy occupies today is not this one. It was raised between 1875 and 1879, after his death, so the pin marks a school and not a room he ever stood in.
suggested_refs: Enrolment records of the Kunstakademie Dusseldorf for the 1790s

stops.name: Dusseldorf, the father dead and the goldsmith refused
stops.date_confidence: disputed. en.wikipedia and the 1911 Britannica put the father's death in 1799; de.wikipedia gives his dates as 1748-1800. Read as c. 1799/1800. The month and day are unrecorded and default to the first.
stops.campa: His father dies and the income stops. The family is large; an elder brother and Peter take it on between them. Advisers press his mother to apprentice the boy to a goldsmith, on the double ground that painting takes too long to learn and that there are painters enough in the world already. She refuses them. He works as a portraitist and an illustrator, paid by the head and by the plate, and keeps drawing, held to it by a fear he later names plainly: that he would be taken away from the art before he had it.
stops.quote: It fell to the lot of an elder brother and myself to watch over the interests of a numerous family. It was at this time that it was attempted to persuade my mother that it would be better for me to devote myself to the trade of a goldsmith than to continue to pursue painting, in the first place, in consequence of the time necessary to qualify me for the art, and in the next, because there were already so many painters. My dear mother, however, rejected all this advice, and I felt myself impelled onward by an uncontrollable enthusiasm, to which the confidence of my mother gave new strength, which was supported by the continual fear that I should be removed from the study of that art I loved so much.
stops.quote_source: Peter von Cornelius, letter to Count Athanasius Raczynski, quoted in English translation, translator uncredited, in the Encyclopaedia Britannica, 11th ed. (1911), vol. 7, 'Cornelius, Peter von', by William Cave Thomas. Verified against the proofread Wikisource text of the page; the original German letter was not located.
suggested_refs: Athanasius Raczynski, Geschichte der neueren deutschen Kunst, which prints Cornelius's autobiographical letters

stops.name: Weimar, the prize competitions of Goethe's circle
stops.date_confidence: attested as a span, 1803 to 1805, per de.wikipedia; the year given opens the span. Coordinate inherited unchanged from goethe_full.journey.json rather than recomputed.
stops.campa: From Weimar the subjects are set and the entries judged, and for a decade the prize competitions organised under Goethe's patronage are the nearest thing the German states have to a national jury. Cornelius sends work into them between 1803 and 1805, an academy student from a provincial Rhineland town aiming at the one address in Germany that confers standing. He does not carry the field. The competitions put his name inside the household of the man whose Faust he will spend the next decade drawing in outline.
suggested_refs: The Weimarer Preisaufgaben and their surviving entry lists, 1799-1805

stops.name: Neuss, the choir of the Quirinus-Munster
stops.date_confidence: contradiction, unresolved. en.wikipedia dates the Neuss commission to 1803; de.wikipedia states that in 1806/08 he made wall paintings in the Quirinus-Munster. The German dating is better supported, since he was still at the Dusseldorf academy until about 1805, but the English date is recorded rather than resolved away. Coordinate corrected to the church's own article coordinates, 51.1991/6.6932.
stops.campa: In the choir of the Quirinus-Munster at Neuss he is given wall to paint, his first monumental commission and his first argument with plaster. The sources fight over when. English Wikipedia dates it to 1803, when he is a student still; German Wikipedia dates it to the years 1806 to 1808. Neither is dropped here. Whatever he painted has not survived: the large choir paintings the church shows now are Franz Ittenbach's, made in 1863 and 1864, and the Munster's own article does not mention Cornelius at all.
suggested_refs: Parish and chapter accounts of St Quirinus, Neuss, for the fabric of the choir, 1803-1808

stops.name: Dusseldorf, the mother's grave
stops.date_confidence: attested, full date given by de.wikipedia.
stops.campa: Anna Helena Corsten dies at Dusseldorf on the second of June. The woman who refused the goldsmith's apprenticeship on her son's behalf does not live to see the art she defended take him out of Germany; he leaves for Frankfurt in the autumn and for Rome two years after that. The city he goes out of has held him for twenty-six years and holds now his father, his training, his first commission and both his parents' graves. He does not work in it again until it sends for him at thirty-six with a directorship in its hand.
suggested_refs: Dusseldorf burial registers for June 1809

segments.name: Frankfurt, and the Outlines to Faust

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the publisher's house
stops.date_confidence: attested as autumn 1809 by de.wikipedia. The month is set to October as the ordinary reading of Herbst and the day defaults to the first; neither is in the source.
stops.campa: In the autumn he moves to Frankfurt am Main and lodges with the publisher Friedrich Wilmans, in whose house he stays until he leaves for Rome. He is twenty-six, out from under the academy for the first time, and living at the address where books are made rather than where pictures are hung. The work he begins here is not painting. It is outline: line without shadow or colour, the whole weight of a scene carried on its contour, a method meant for the copperplate and for a public that buys prints rather than walls.
suggested_refs: The publishing house of Friedrich Wilmans at Frankfurt, and its correspondence for 1809-1811

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the outlines to Faust
stops.date_confidence: attested that the Faust illustrations are begun at Frankfurt from 1809 (en.wikipedia); the plates appear as Bilder zu Goethes Faust between 1816 and 1826. The year here is a placeholder inside the Frankfurt residence.
stops.campa: He draws Goethe's Faust, a cycle that ends as twelve plates and is published between 1816 and 1826 under the title Bilder zu Goethes Faust. The poem is thirty years in the making and its author is alive in Weimar, reading what is made of him. Cornelius takes the German subject at the moment the German states are deciding they have a literature, and he takes it in outline, the plainest and most portable of methods. The drawings go south with him in 1811, and the plates go out across Germany while he is living in Rome.
suggested_refs: Bilder zu Goethes Faust, twelve engraved plates, published 1816-1826

segments.name: The Road South and the Convent of Sant'Isidoro

stops.name: Innsbruck, the crossing that is not documented
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. No source consulted documents Cornelius's route between Frankfurt and Rome. The stop is the standard early-nineteenth-century German artists' road to Italy and is tagged as inference; month and day are arbitrary.
stops.campa: The road he takes south is written down nowhere reachable. German painters of his generation go over the Tyrol, through Innsbruck and the Brenner, because that is the road; Overbeck's party crossed it the year before on the same errand. The pin rests on that reasoning and on nothing else, and it should be moved without argument the moment a letter turns up with a different itinerary. The companion is attested, and the destination, and the day of arrival. No league of the road between them is attested at all.
sources: reconstruction, standard Grand Tour route; not verified in any source consulted
johann_friedrich_overbeck.journey.json (corpus, 1810 Brenner crossing, itself marked as reconstruction)
suggested_refs: Passport and post-house records of the Tyrol road for 1811

stops.name: Florence, the inherited gap
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. No source places Cornelius in Florence in 1811. The coordinate is inherited byte-identical from johann_friedrich_overbeck.journey.json, where the same waypoint is recorded explicitly as a gap rather than a document.
stops.campa: Florence lies on the same conventional road, and the pin here is Overbeck's, taken from the corpus unaltered, where it was set for the identical reason and marked as a gap. Two parties of young Germans go down to Rome a year apart, both of them hunting the painting made before Raphael, and neither leaves a source saying whether they stopped in the city that holds most of it. The reconstruction is entered so that no later reader mistakes a plausible road for a recorded one.
sources: reconstruction, standard travel route; not verified this session
suggested_refs: Letters of the Roman German colony for 1811, which might name the stages of Cornelius's journey

stops.name: Rome, the fourteenth of October
stops.date_confidence: attested, full date given by the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica; de.wikipedia gives the year and the travelling companion.
stops.campa: He enters Rome on the fourteenth of October in the company of the painter Christian Xeller, carrying the Faust drawings and no commission. The city holds a colony of German painters, and inside it a brotherhood one year old on Roman ground: Johann Friedrich Overbeck, Franz Pforr, Ludwig Vogel, Johann Konrad Hottinger, thrown out of the Vienna academy and living in a half-emptied convent. Cornelius is twenty-eight, older than any of them, and arrives not as a disciple but as a man with a method already finished.
suggested_refs: Roman police and stato d'anime registers of foreigners for October 1811

stops.name: Rome, the convent of Sant'Isidoro a Capo le Case
stops.date_confidence: attested that he joins the Lukasbund after arriving in Rome in 1811; no source gives the day, which is set to the week following his documented arrival. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from johann_friedrich_overbeck.journey.json and franz_pforr.journey.json.
stops.campa: The Franciscan convent of Sant'Isidoro on the slope below the Pincio has empty cells and the brotherhood has taken four of them. Cornelius joins the Lukasbund here, two years after its founding at the Vienna academy and one year after four of its members carried it over the Alps. He does not take the monkish pose as far as some of them do. He takes the programme: outline before colour, the German fifteenth century and the Italian one before Raphael, painting understood as a public and religious art rather than a cabinet trade.
suggested_refs: The convent of Sant'Isidoro a Capo le Case and the Lukasbund's occupation of its cells from 1810

stops.name: Rome, the quarter below the Trinita dei Monti
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as to Cornelius specifically. The quarter is the German painters' quarter and the brotherhood occupies it from 1810; no source gives Cornelius an address in it. The coordinate is inherited byte-identical from johann_friedrich_overbeck.journey.json, where it is itself Tischbein's 1779 pin, inherited without alteration.
stops.campa: The streets between the Spanish Steps and the Via Sistina are the German painters' quarter and have been for a generation. Johann Heinrich Wilhelm Tischbein lodged in them in 1779, and the pin here is Tischbein's, passed down the corpus untouched; the Nazarenes occupy the same few hundred metres from 1810. No source gives Cornelius a door. It gives him a quarter, and the quarter is small enough that a door would add little to it. He works in a foreign city inside a German village four streets wide.
suggested_refs: The German artists' quarter below the Trinita dei Monti, occupied continuously from Tischbein's generation to the Nazarenes

stops.name: Rome, the apartment on the Via del Corso
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as to Cornelius. franz_pforr.journey.json records the brotherhood taking an apartment on the Via del Corso in 1811; no source in the corpus places Cornelius's own lodging there. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from that file.
stops.campa: The brotherhood takes an apartment on the Via del Corso in the year Cornelius arrives, a quarter of an hour down the hill from the convent. Goethe kept house on this street in 1786 with Tischbein and counted his entry into Rome a second birth. Cornelius, who has spent two years drawing Goethe's Faust, is now at work a few doors from where the poem's author took his own Italian cure. No source puts Cornelius at either address. The pin comes from Pforr's file, and the two tenancies stand twenty-five years apart in any case.
suggested_refs: The Casa di Goethe on the Via del Corso, occupied 1786-1788

stops.name: Rome, Sant'Isidoro: Pforr dies and the household ends
stops.date_confidence: the death is 1812. The day here is inherited from franz_pforr.journey.json rather than independently established, because the research pool records the year only. The dissolution that follows is dated by de.wikipedia's Lukasbund article: Vogel and Hottinger leave Rome in 1813.
stops.campa: Franz Pforr dies in the convent at twenty-four, having painted almost nothing and having formed the brotherhood's mind more than anyone except Overbeck. The community comes apart behind him: Vogel and Hottinger leave Rome the following year, and the communal phase at Sant'Isidoro is over long before the decade is. Cornelius and Wilhelm von Schadow stay. In Pforr's own file this stop is a death; here it is where the brotherhood stops being a household and becomes a school.
suggested_refs: The dispersal of the Lukasbund from Sant'Isidoro, 1812-1813

stops.name: Rome, the marriage to Carolina Grossi
stops.date_confidence: attested year, 1814, per de.wikipedia; the month and day are unrecorded and default to the first.
stops.campa: He marries Carolina Grossi, born in Rome, three years after arriving in the city. The member of the brotherhood who kept the least monastic discipline takes an Italian wife and a household, and the marriage lasts twenty years, until she dies in Munich in 1834. She is the first of three, two of them Roman and the third from Urbino. The son of a Dusseldorf gallery inspector, who will spend his working life making a German national art on Bavarian and Prussian plaster, is married to Italy from twenty-nine until his death.
suggested_refs: Roman parish marriage registers for 1814, which would give Carolina Grossi's family and quarter

segments.name: The Walls of the Palazzo Zuccari

stops.name: Naples, the excursion that is only tradition
stops.date_confidence: unverified tradition. No source consulted places Cornelius in Naples, gives a date, or names an occasion. The year is arbitrary within the period c. 1812-1818 and the stop is tagged as reconstruction.
stops.campa: Tradition puts the Roman Germans on the Naples road at least once in these years, for the bay, the antiquities, and the Greek temples further south. No source consulted names a date or an occasion for Cornelius. The stop is entered because the absence deserves marking: eight years of his life in Italy are documented almost entirely by commissions, and the ordinary movement of a working painter between them leaves no trace whatever in the encyclopedias that carry him.
sources: unverified tradition, general Nazarene-circle practice; not confirmed in any source consulted
suggested_refs: Sketchbooks and letters of the Roman Nazarenes recording excursions to Naples and Paestum

stops.name: Rome, Palazzo Zuccari: the story of Joseph
stops.date_confidence: en.wikipedia (Nazarene movement) dates the Casa Bartholdy Joseph frescoes to 1816-17; de.wikipedia dates the commission to 1815. One item in the research pool dated this work to 1811, an error of four to six years, corrected here. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from johann_friedrich_overbeck.journey.json.
stops.campa: Jakob Salomon Bartholdy, Prussian consul general, rents rooms in the Palazzo Zuccari on the Via Gregoriana and gives four Germans a wall apiece. Overbeck takes Joseph sold by his brethren and the seven years of famine; Cornelius, Philipp Veit and Wilhelm von Schadow take the rest of the story. It is buon fresco, recovered out of books and ruins by men who have never painted it, and it carries the Nazarene name across Europe. Cornelius paints here what he will paint for forty years after: wall, not canvas.
stops.quote: Overbeck from Lubeck is the one who by the gentleness and nobility of his soul draws all around him
stops.quote_source: Peter von Cornelius on Friedrich Overbeck, cited to Atkinson (1882), p. 20, via johann_friedrich_overbeck.journey.json; the original German has not been independently located.
suggested_refs: The Casa Bartholdy Joseph cycle, Alte Nationalgalerie, Berlin, detached from the Palazzo Zuccari in 1886-87

stops.name: Rome, the Faust plates and the Nibelungen outlines
stops.date_confidence: attested. The Nibelungen designs are dated 1817 (Aventiure von den Nibelungen, de.wikipedia); the Faust cycle is published in instalments 1816-1826, and de.wikipedia records the completed series appearing from 1816.
stops.campa: The Faust plates begin to appear, engraved out of the Frankfurt outlines, and in 1817 he draws the Aventiure von den Nibelungen. He is illustrating the two poems Germany is in the act of deciding are its own: one written by a living minister of state at Weimar, the other by nobody at all, surviving in manuscript. The Nazarene programme held that painting should serve religion. In Cornelius's hands, in Rome, it starts serving a literature, which in the German states in 1817 is very nearly the same office.
suggested_refs: Aventiure von den Nibelungen, outline designs, 1817
Bilder zu Goethes Faust, published 1816-1826

stops.name: Rome, the Casino Massimo: the Dante room unpainted
stops.date_confidence: contradiction, flagged. en.wikipedia lists the Villa Massimi among Cornelius's Roman decorations; it.wikipedia (Casino Massimo Lancellotti) records Philipp Veit painting the Paradiso on the vault and Joseph Anton Koch the Inferno and Purgatorio on the four walls, 1818-28. The assignment to Cornelius is attested, his execution of it is not. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from johann_friedrich_overbeck.journey.json.
stops.campa: Prince Massimo gives the brotherhood the walls of his garden casino: a room of Tasso to Overbeck, a room of Ariosto to Veit, a room of Dante to Cornelius. Cornelius does not paint it. He goes to Munich in 1819 with the room unbegun, and Veit takes the Paradiso on the vault while Joseph Anton Koch paints the Inferno and the Purgatorio across the four walls between 1818 and 1828. English Wikipedia still credits Cornelius with decorating the place. The Italian article on the casino names Veit and Koch and not him.
suggested_refs: The Casino Massimo Lancellotti and its Tasso, Ariosto and Dante rooms, 1817-1828

stops.name: Munich, the Residenz: the Crown Prince sends for him
stops.date_confidence: attested year, 1819, in both en.wikipedia and de.wikipedia; the month and day are unrecorded and default to the first.
stops.campa: Crown Prince Ludwig of Bavaria, who has been buying antiquities in Rome and raising a house for them on the Konigsplatz, wants the Glyptothek's halls painted and sends for Cornelius. The summons closes the Roman decade. Overbeck stays in Rome and will die there; Cornelius goes north to work for a state, and the brotherhood that met in a convent begins its second life inside royal academies. He is thirty-six, and the wall he is offered is larger than anything Rome ever put in front of him.
suggested_refs: Ludwig of Bavaria's Roman correspondence on the decoration of the Glyptothek

stops.name: Dusseldorf, the directorship of the academy
stops.date_confidence: contradiction, unresolved. de.wikipedia's Kunstakademie Dusseldorf article records him as director from 1 October 1819 to 1825, with Mosler as interim in 1825-26; en.wikipedia dates the directorship 1821-1824. Both are carried. Coordinate corrected to Eiskellerstrasse 1, approximately 51.2288/6.7716; the present building dates from 1875-79 and is not the house he ran.
stops.campa: He takes the direction of the Kunstakademie Dusseldorf, appointed from the first of October, and holds it while the Munich work goes forward under his cartoons. It is the school he entered as a boy in his father's shadow, and he comes back to it as its head. The sources disagree about the years: the German account gives 1819 to 1825, the English gives 1821 to 1824, and no document reachable here decides between them. Both readings are recorded and neither is dissolved into the other.
suggested_refs: Prussian ministerial files on the reorganisation of the Dusseldorf academy, 1819-1826

stops.name: Munich, the Glyptothek: the gods of Greece
stops.date_confidence: attested as a span, 1820 to 1830, per de.wikipedia; the year given opens the span.
stops.campa: In the Glyptothek on the Konigsplatz he paints the gods and the heroes across two halls, the Gottersaal and the Heroensaal, ten years of work carried out in large part by pupils working under his cartoons. It is fresco on the Roman method laid onto a German museum built to hold Greek marbles. The scaffolding is itself a school: the men who serve their years under him here are the ones the other German academies hire, and the method travels out of Munich in their hands rather than in his.
suggested_refs: The Glyptothek's Gottersaal and Heroensaal fresco cycles, 1820-1830

stops.name: Munich, the academy after Langer
stops.date_confidence: Langer's death on 6 August 1824 is attested (de.wikipedia); the sources give the transition to Cornelius as 1824-1825. Coordinate is the Akademie der Bildenden Kunste at Akademiestrasse 2-4, 48.1531/11.5803, corrected from the pool; the Neureuther building on that site was raised 1876-85 and occupied only from 1886, so it is not the house Cornelius directed.
stops.campa: Johann Peter von Langer, director of the Munich academy, dies on the sixth of August, and Cornelius is named in his place, giving up Dusseldorf to Wilhelm von Schadow. The two chief academies of Germany are now held by two men who met in a Roman convent. Overbeck, offered Munich and afterwards the Stadelsches Kunstinstitut at Frankfurt, refuses both and stays in Rome painting; his file records the refusals. Cornelius takes the office, and with it everything an office does to a programme.
suggested_refs: Bavarian court records of the succession to Langer at the Munich academy, 1824-1825

stops.name: Munich, the particle
stops.date_confidence: attested year, 1825, per de.wikipedia, for both the formal appointment and the ennoblement; the month and day are unrecorded and default to the first.
stops.campa: Ludwig I, a year on the throne, confirms him formally in the academy's direction and ennobles him. Peter Cornelius becomes Peter von Cornelius. The son of a gallery inspector, who was very nearly apprenticed to a goldsmith on the argument that painting took too long to learn, is made noble by a king whose walls he paints. The particle is a measure of what the Bavarian building programme is worth to the crown, and of what the crown expects to be handed back in plaster.
suggested_refs: Bavarian patents of nobility for 1825

stops.name: Munich, the Pinakothek and the history of art
stops.date_confidence: the pool gives the Pinakothek involvement as c. 1826-1836 without a precise start; the year is a placeholder. The posthumous publication date, 1875, is attested by de.wikipedia.
stops.campa: For Leo von Klenze's new Pinakothek he designs a fresco cycle on the history of art itself: painting made the subject of painting, on the way in to the pictures, in a gallery raised to hang the Wittelsbach collection. The designs are published in 1875 as Entwurfe zu den kunstgeschichtlichen Fresken, eight years after his death and by other men's decision. He leaves at this pin a plan for a museum that explains its own contents in pictures before the visitor reaches them.
suggested_refs: Entwurfe zu den kunstgeschichtlichen Fresken, published Munich 1875

stops.name: Munich, the death of Carolina and a daughter
stops.date_confidence: attested, full date given by de.wikipedia for both deaths.
stops.campa: On the twenty-fourth of October his wife Carolina and a daughter die. He is fifty-one, in the middle of the Bavarian programme, with the Ludwigskirche wall still ahead of him. The German article records the two deaths in a single line and nothing further: no letter, no account of the household, not even the daughter's name reached this research. The gap is left where it is, because it is the shape of the sources on him. The commissions are documented to the year and the family to the date only.
suggested_refs: Munich burial registers for October 1834

stops.name: Munich, the Ludwigskirche: the Last Judgment
stops.date_confidence: attested as a span, 1836 to 1840, per de.wikipedia (St. Ludwig, Munchen); the year given opens the span. Dimensions of roughly 62 feet by 38 are the 1911 Britannica's report and are not independently checked. Coordinate corrected to 48.1489/11.5814 from the pool's 48.15/11.5822, about 140 m off.
stops.campa: Over the high altar of the Ludwigskirche he paints the Last Judgment, reported by the 1911 Britannica at sixty-two feet in height by thirty-eight in width, worked between 1836 and 1840. The German article calls it the second largest altar fresco in the world after Michelangelo's. It is the thing the convent programme was written to produce: a public religious painting on a wall, at the scale of its own subject, in a church built for it by a king who wanted one and could pay.
suggested_refs: The choir fresco of the Last Judgment, St Ludwig, Munich, 1836-1840

segments.name: The Building That Is Never Built

stops.name: Berlin, the break with Ludwig
stops.date_confidence: contradiction, unresolved. de.wikipedia dates the quarrel with Ludwig I and the move to Berlin to 1841; en.wikipedia puts the Munich to Berlin move earlier, about 1839-1840. The German date is carried and the English one is recorded, not dissolved.
stops.campa: He falls out with Ludwig I and leaves Munich for Berlin. The German article dates the break to 1841, the English one puts the move two years earlier, and neither gives the occasion of the quarrel. The shape of it is plain enough. The painter the whole Bavarian programme was built around walks out of it at fifty-eight, leaves the Glyptothek and the Ludwigskirche behind him at the height of both, and takes service with the other German crown that is buying pictures at that scale.
suggested_refs: Correspondence between Ludwig I and Cornelius, 1839-1841, on the terms of the Munich commissions

stops.name: Berlin, the Campo Santo cartoons begun
stops.date_confidence: attested that the commission is Frederick William IV's and that work runs from 1841 to 1867 (de.wikipedia and en.wikipedia); the month is a placeholder inside 1841.
stops.campa: Frederick William IV of Prussia intends a Campo Santo beside the cathedral, a royal burial hall painted through with the Apocalypse, and brings Cornelius to Berlin to design it. He begins the cartoons: the riders of the Apocalypse at full size, charcoal and chalk on paper, drawn to be transferred to walls that do not exist. He is fifty-eight when he starts. He is still enlarging them at eighty-four, and by then no stone of the building has been laid and none ever will be.
suggested_refs: The Apocalyptic Riders cartoons for the Berlin Campo Santo, drawn 1841-1867

stops.name: London, the Palace of Westminster
stops.date_confidence: attested to November 1841 by en.wikipedia; the day is unrecorded and defaults to the first.
stops.campa: In November he crosses to England at the invitation of the Fine Arts Commission, which is deciding whether the rebuilt Houses of Parliament should be frescoed and has no fresco painter in the kingdom to consult. They send for a German. The method they are asking about was recovered twenty-five years earlier by four young men in a Prussian consul's rented rooms on the Via Gregoriana, and the man standing in front of the commission is one of the four who put it back on a wall.
suggested_refs: Reports of the Royal Fine Arts Commission on fresco for the new Palace of Westminster, 1841-1843

stops.name: Berlin, the Lawless Society
stops.date_confidence: attested year, 1843, per de.wikipedia; the month and day are unrecorded and default to the first.
stops.campa: He joins the Gesetzlose Gesellschaft of Berlin, the Lawless Society, a social circle whose name is a joke about having no statutes to break. The convent painter of 1811, who wore the Nazarene programme like an order of religion, is at sixty a fixture of the Prussian capital's table. Nothing said at those tables reached this research. The membership is attested and the talk is not, which is the record a man leaves once he has finished turning into an institution.
suggested_refs: Membership rolls of the Berlin Gesetzlose Gesellschaft, founded 1809

stops.name: Berlin, the mausoleum dropped
stops.date_confidence: attested that the Campo Santo project is abandoned after 1848 and that Cornelius continued the cartoons to 1867 (de.wikipedia, en.wikipedia). The month is a placeholder inside the revolutionary year.
stops.campa: The revolution comes and Frederick William IV drops the Campo Santo. There will be no mausoleum, no walls, and no transfer of the cartoons to plaster. Cornelius goes on drawing them regardless, at full size, for another nineteen years. The cartoons survive and are the work his name carries longest; the commission that produced them was cancelled when he was sixty-five. He is offered no substitute for it and asks for none, and the Apocalypse grows on paper in a studio.

Both cannot be true. The late Roman residence is entered here as unreliable rather than deleted, because something inside it is probably sound: a man who spent his thirties in this city, married two Roman wives and had the freedom of its German colony did not simply stop returning to it. The town that could not keep him claims him anyway. stops.name: Berlin, death in the eighty-fourth year
stops.date_confidence: attested, full date, agreed by de.wikipedia, en.wikipedia and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is this date that contradicts en.wikipedia's own claim of a Roman residence running to 1869.
stops.campa: Peter von Cornelius dies at Berlin on the sixth of March. The Apocalypse cartoons stand in the studio, finished as far as anything can be finished that has no wall waiting for it, and the Campo Santo has been dead paper for nineteen years. He has outlived Pforr by fifty-five years and Overbeck will outlive him by two. Of the men who took cells at Sant'Isidoro, he is the one who accepted every office a state offered him, and the state's building was never begun.
